title: Vitamin C facilitates direct cardiac reprogramming by inhibiting reactive oxygen species

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods, Statistical Analysis section (end of Methods)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states: 'Data were analyzed with GraphPad Prism 9, and comparisons were performed with a t-test (non-parametric tests) and a two-way ANOVA.' This phrasing incorrectly characterizes the t-test as a non-parametric test. A standard t-test is a parametric test that assumes normally distributed data; non-parametric equivalents (e.g., Mann-Whitney U) are distinct tests. Labeling the t-test itself as 'non-parametric' is a factual/statistical terminology error that a careful reviewer would ask to be corrected or clarified.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract vs. Methods (MEF spheroid formation section)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims: 'We found that vitamin C (VitC) significantly increased cardiac reprogramming efficiency when added to GMT-overexpressing fibroblasts from human and mice in 2D and 3D model.' However, the Methods section only describes a 3D spheroid protocol for 'MEFs spheroid formation' (mouse cells, using the αMHC-GFP reporter), with no corresponding 3D/spheroid protocol described for human fetal cardiac fibroblasts (hFCFs). This creates an inconsistency between the claim that both human and mouse fibroblasts were tested in a 3D model and the methodology, which only supports a 3D experiment for mouse cells.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph beginning 'Here, we present the first evidence...'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states: 'Here, we present the first evidence that Vitamin C (VitC) significantly promotes the direct reprogramming of fibroblasts by GMT into cardiomyocytes, partially mediated by reactive oxygen species (ROS) reduction.' This is an unsupported/overstated novelty claim: the same introduction notes that VitC was already a known enhancer of 'cardiomyocyte differentiation or hiPSC reprogramming' (citations 19–25), and other literature has previously examined small-molecule/antioxidant enhancement of direct cardiac reprogramming. Declaring 'first evidence' without acknowledging or ruling out prior related work overstates the novelty of the finding.

The text specifies: 'The screening criteria for DEGs were P-value < 10⁻⁶ and Log2 fold change ≥ 0.5 and ≤ (−0.5).' Using an extremely stringent raw (unadjusted) p-value threshold of 10⁻⁶ is unconventional for RNA-seq DEG calling (typical practice uses FDR/adjusted p-value thresholds such as padj < 0.05 from DESeq2), while later in the same Methods section GSEA is evaluated using an FDR-based threshold (FDR < 0.1). The inconsistent use of an uncorrected, unusually strict p-value cutoff for DEGs alongside an FDR-corrected cutoff for GSEA represents an internally inconsistent statistical methodology that is not adequately justified.
